topic: Prove-It: Adversarial Verification Agent Skill for Claude Code

competitors.name: Pablo-aps/prove-it (anchor)
key_points: The subject of the article: a single-file, Apache-2.0 Agent Skill that makes an agent falsify its own 'done' claim instead of collecting confirming signals.

Four-rule loop: DEFINE (freeze a falsifiable claim + acceptance criteria) -> BREAK (make a ranked falsification plan) -> VERIFY (verify the outcome, not a proxy) -> VERDICT (PROVEN / FAILED / NOT PROVEN / BLOCKED).

Tagline/reframe: 'Don't try to prove it works. Try to prove it doesn't.' Installs via `npx skills add Pablo-aps/prove-it`; manual install drops skills/prove-it/SKILL.md into .claude/skills/prove-it/, .agents/skills/prove-it/, or .cursor/skills/prove-it/.
Explicitly out of scope: no runtime dependencies, hooks, background process, telemetry, MCP server, or orchestration layer. It is a behavioral guardrail, not a test framework or security scanner.

Ships a 12-case reproducible benchmark (3 positive controls) with verdict accuracy, false-assurance rate, decisive-signal recall and positive-control accuracy; published 2026-08-18 Codex result is self-authored, not independent evaluation.

Flags 'counterfeit proof' patterns: test.skip/xit, ignored exit codes, removed or weakened assertions, empty catches, `|| true`, blanket suppressions, hardcoded results, unrelated mocks, timeout increases without a reproduced timing cause.
Names the anti-pattern 'vibe verification': an agent sees enough green signals to feel confident and stops searching for ways the conclusion could be false.
Self-described 'open-source adversarial verification Agent Skill for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor' — this repo IS the keyword.
Tagline and doctrine: 'Don't try to prove it works. Try to prove it doesn't.'

Four rules, one verdict: 01 DEFINE (turn 'looks fixed' into a falsifiable claim; freeze scope + acceptance criteria) -> 02 BREAK (ask what would contradict the claim; run decisive safe checks first) -> 03 VERIFY (verify the real outcome, not a proxy such as exit code / HTTP 200 / green healthcheck) -> 04 VERDICT.
Four verdicts: PROVEN / FAILED / NOT PROVEN / BLOCKED. PROVEN is deliberately scoped — no claim of mathematical proof, universal correctness or future safety.
Coins 'vibe verification': 'when an agent sees enough positive signals to feel confident and stops searching for ways the conclusion could be false.'
Ships a reproducible 12-case benchmark (misleading green signals -> FAILED; incomplete evidence -> NOT PROVEN; inaccessible evidence -> BLOCKED; 3 positive controls -> PROVEN).

Published benchmark delta (Codex CLI 0.147.0, gpt-5.6-luna, low reasoning, 2026-08-18, 1 run/cell): verdict accuracy 9/12 (75%) baseline -> 12/12 (100%) with skill; positive controls 2/3 (67%) -> 3/3 (100%); false assurance 0/12 both arms.
Authors flag the benchmark honestly: cases were authored during skill development, so it is a regression test, not an independent evaluation; one run per cell is 'directional evidence'.
Zero runtime dependencies; single portable SKILL.md following the open Agent Skills spec; install via `npx skills add Pablo-aps/prove-it`; listed at skills.sh/pablo-aps/prove-it/prove-it.

Per-agent install + invocation table: Claude Code `.claude/skills/prove-it/SKILL.md` -> `/prove-it`; Codex `.agents/skills/prove-it/SKILL.md` -> `$prove-it`; Cursor `.cursor/skills/prove-it/SKILL.md`.

Counterfeit-proof taxonomy in README: skipped tests, weakened assertions, ignored exit codes, empty catches, hardcoded results, behavior mocked away, timeouts increased without reproducing the timing failure.

The 'expensive kind of done' table: tests green != original bug fixed; build green != deployment works; deploy succeeded != every replica runs the new version; healthcheck 200 != workers/dependencies healthy; HTTP 200 != async operation completed; no errors in these logs != no relevant error occurred; one successful request != race condition fixed; agent confidence != evidence.

SKILL.md integrity rules: verify read-only by default (no mutating prod, no destroying data, no weakening controls to obtain proof); freeze the claim BEFORE inspecting evidence; do not make the claim easier after a check fails; label facts KNOWN / INFERRED / UNKNOWN; treat prior conclusions (including the agent's own) as claims, not evidence.
Multi-language READMEs (zh-CN, pt-BR, ja, es, ru) — signals international distribution intent.
Closest neighbor by name and intent (198 stars, MIT). Hook-based, Claude Code only: installs lifecycle hooks that BLOCK the agent from stopping or committing until configured tasks pass.
Config-driven JSON tasks: script and subagent tasks, AI reviewers as independent subagents, async reviews, churn/signal gating, tool-use guards, run de-duplication.
Ships /prove skill plus prove-approach and prove-coverage reviewer prompts; explicit PASS/FAIL verdict from a separate process that has no stake in the code it judges.

Contrast for the article: prove_it enforces verification mechanically at the harness level (cannot be skipped), whereas Prove It is a portable prompt-level discipline that works across Claude Code, Codex and Cursor with zero runtime.

competitors.name: danpeg/bug-hunt
key_points: Adversarial bug hunting skill (146 stars, MIT) using 3 isolated agents with no shared context: Hunter (over-reports every possible bug), Skeptic (biased to disprove), Referee (independently reads code and issues final verdicts).
Inspired by exploiting LLM sycophancy for better code review; isolation between agents prevents anchoring bias.

Scoring incentives are load-bearing: Hunter +1/+5/+10 by severity; Skeptic earns points for disproving but pays a 2x penalty for wrongly dismissing real bugs; Referee uses symmetric +1/-1 'ground truth' framing.
Supports whole-project, directory/file, and branch-diff scan modes (-b branch --base main), reading full file contents rather than just the diff.
Contrast: multi-agent orchestration vs Prove It's single-skill falsification; bug-hunt finds bugs, Prove It adjudicates claims.
Most-starred adversarial-verification skill in this niche (146 stars, 12 forks) — the SERP/credibility leader and the strongest 'alternative' to compare against.
3 isolated agents: Hunter (over-reports every possible bug) -> Skeptic (disproves each, biased to dismiss false positives) -> Referee (reads code independently, final verdict).
Load-bearing design choice: each agent runs in a COMPLETELY ISOLATED context — they never see each other's reasoning, only structured findings. This prevents anchoring bias.

Scoring incentives are the mechanism, not window dressing: Hunter +1/+5/+10 for low/medium/critical; Skeptic earns for disproving but pays a 2x penalty for wrongly dismissing a real bug; Referee uses symmetric +1/-1 with 'ground truth' framing.
Scope control: `/bug-hunt`, `/bug-hunt src/`, `/bug-hunt -b feature-xyz [--base dev]` for branch-diff mode; reads full file contents (not just the diff) so detection quality holds.
Attribution: based on @systematicls's technique write-up on exploiting LLM sycophancy for better code review (X/Twitter, 2026-03).
Install is a plain git clone into ~/.claude/skills/ — no marketplace dependency.

competitors.name: fullo/claude-adversarial-skill
key_points: Claude Code skill performing adversarial verification with Chain-of-Verification (CoV) plus abstractive red-teaming, hidden-behaviour probing, stress techniques and tri-modal reasoning.

Protocol: decompose artifacts into verifiable claims, classify each as deductive/inductive/abductive, generate adversarial questions ('what would make this fail?'), trace actual execution paths, then report with confidence scoring.
Verification domains span code, architecture, data/migrations, documentation, tests and other agents' analysis output.
Includes agent meta-verification against sycophantic deference, anchoring bias, confabulated confidence, premature convergence and evidence cherry-picking.
Contrast: heavyweight, multi-domain protocol vs Prove It's deliberately small four-step loop and four-verdict output.
Most theoretically explicit of the family: Chain-of-Verification (CoV, Dhuliawala et al. 2023) + abstractive red-teaming + hidden-behavior probing + stress techniques + tri-modal reasoning.

Protocol: decompose artifacts into individual verifiable CLAIMS -> classify each claim's reasoning mode (deductive / inductive / abductive) -> generate adversarial questions ('what would make this fail?') -> abstract individual bugs up to failure CATEGORIES.

Tri-modal confidence scoring is the differentiator: deductive 80-100 (source cited), inductive 60-79 (3+ instances), abductive 40-59 (hypothesis with alternatives). Hard constraint: no score above 79 without a specific file/line/doc citation — an 'anti-fabrication' discipline that generalizes beyond code.
Abductive findings are reported as HYPOTHESES with alternative explanations and proposed tests, never as verified facts.
Verification domains table: code, architecture, data/migrations/contracts, documentation, tests, analysis/agent reports.

Chaos-engineering-inspired stress techniques with forced variety (min 3 per run, never repeat): Existence Question, Scale Shift (what at 10x? at zero?), Time Travel (what in 6 months?), Requirement Inversion.
Reports 'Survived: yes/no' — survived stress tests are treated as first-class output, not wasted effort.
Has a meta-verification section for verifying OTHER agents' outputs: sycophancy, hidden agenda, anchoring bias, confabulated confidence, premature convergence, evidence cherry-picking.
Ships the 'absence probing' rule: before claiming something does not exist, you must state where you looked.

Fable Method (fable-judge skill) treats every completion report as HOSTILE TESTIMONY: extract verification claims, re-execute each claimed check, diff reported vs actual output, diff claimed vs actual git diff.
Flags discrepancies as fraud, not errors; has a fraud table (e.g. claimed 'tests pass' but 2/5 failed -> reject).
Verdicts are VERIFIED / VERIFIED WITH CAVEATS / REFUTED; a claim that cannot be re-run is labelled UNVERIFIABLE, never assumed true.
Its documented failure mode is the same one Prove It targets: coding agents claiming success regardless of reality, tests quietly weakened until they pass, scope silently expanded.
Contrast: re-execution-based judging of another agent's work vs Prove It's self-applied falsification gate before a 'done' claim is trusted.

Skill set for long unattended agent runs (63 stars, MIT); four-phase loop plan -> implement -> verify -> ship and monitor, gated on real checks (lint, tests, benchmarks, manual cURL/browser testing, independent code review, PR monitoring).
Teaches the agent to validate its own work with automated checks and adversarial reviews; stops when acceptance criteria and quality gates pass, or when it can name a blocker.
Configuration via a project-root BACKPRESSURE.md that is authoritative and layers on top of defaults.
Contrast: process/longevity scaffolding around verification vs a portable verification primitive you invoke on a single claim.
Three-agent adversarial verification skill (issue-finder / disprover / judge) with explicitly competing incentives; triggers on 'verify', 'double check', 'are you sure', 'poke holes'.
Recommended for security-sensitive code (auth, crypto, permissions), data integrity (migrations, schema, ETL) and financial logic (payments, billing), i.e. high-blast-radius changes.
Publishes red-flag phrases that mean verification is NOT complete: 'should work', 'probably', 'I think', 'Done!', 'All good!', 'I don't see any issues'.
Notes all-Claude panels share blind spots and suggests adding a cross-model finder (Codex) to the panel when available.
Contrast: named risk tiers and competing-incentive panels vs Prove It's judgement that the agent applies to itself.

competitors.name: apoorvjain25/production-audit
key_points: Convergence-based adversarial audit rather than a single adversarial pass: it keeps sweeping new 'lenses' until the work stops finding things — 24 audit lenses, 18 defect classes.
Claim to authority: 1,200+ real findings on a production B2B SaaS, then 14 verification passes AFTER the fixes before it could honestly say 'done'.

Loop: Phase 0 inventory (every page, claim, endpoint, job, prompt, icon, email, locale) -> pick a never-used lens -> sweep the whole inventory -> verify each candidate finding against real code (trace the guard, run the test that settles it) -> stop only on two consecutive passes with nothing new.
Fix mode adds waves (CRITICAL+HIGH -> MEDIUM -> LOW), a gate (build + typecheck + lint + tests) then an over-reach review, and re-audit with fresh lenses.
Convergence exit criterion is explicit and measurable: two consecutive passes with zero CRITICAL / zero HIGH.
Runs in Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, aider as well as Claude Code (PROMPT.md).
Key contrast to prove-it: production-audit generates and converges on findings; prove-it adjudicates a specific claim already made. Both answer 'is done real?' from opposite directions.

competitors.name: henchmarketing-rgb/sub-zero-skill
key_points: Hardest version of the 'separate verifier' thesis: the verifier must be a SEPARATE, FRESH-CONTEXT agent that checks the actual world (fetches the URL, takes the screenshot, checks the git ref) — only the verifier can call a win, and it has never seen the work, only the result.

'No evidence, no win.' Core diagnosis: 'The agent grading its own homework is the problem. "Tests pass" is something a model can convince itself of. "The URL returns 200 with the pricing table on screen" is not.'
Two modes from one command: Audit (cold read of git state, build, tests, lint, deployment, a live visual sweep, and doc-vs-reality drift) and verify-a-claim.
Extreme 'cold' persona/tone — useful as a contrast example of a skill where persona is doing the enforcement work rather than a schema.

competitors.name: jkaraml/prove-it (name-collision competitor)
key_points: Same name, narrower scope: 'a Claude Code skill that won't let your agent say "done" without proof.'

Enforces 5 rules: run the thing (not the tests around it); run what the project already has (tests/typecheck/lint); prove the fix fixes (show it failing first, then passing); try to break it (empty, zero, missing, huge); re-read the request and say out loud what you skipped.
Bans a specific phrase list that 'means I didn't run it': should work, looks correct, this is straightforward.
Its 'Before/After' transcript is the best copywriting in the niche: 'Not done: the `per_page` parameter. You mentioned it; I did not build it.' — explicit partial-completion honesty.

competitors.name: josharsh/prove-it
key_points: Specializes on 'test theater': challenges tests to actually catch bugs, detects weak assertions, test theater, and missing edge cases.
Evidence that 'prove-it' as a skill name is converging into a genre with sub-specializations (test adequacy, UI proof, general falsification).

competitors.name: jongouveia/prove-it
key_points: Framed around model distrust of its own completion: makes the model distrust its own 'done' and hunt for the bugs a confident finish hides.

competitors.name: ng/adversarial-review
key_points: Dual-agent adversarial code review plugin: 'The Optimizer' and 'The Skeptic' review independently and challenge each other; only findings that survive the challenge at high confidence get auto-fixed.
Distinctive mechanic: cross-vendor agreement — optional OpenAI Codex reviewer, so agreement ACROSS providers becomes the strongest signal.
Cost-gated by design: free mechanical checks (lint/typecheck/build/test) run first, then a weighted escalation score decides 2-agent (standard) or 4-agent (full) depth.
Bounded verify loop (max 2 iterations) catches regressions introduced by the auto-fixes themselves.

Explicitly positions against Claude Code's built-in /code-review: 'adversarial verification — a second pass (The Skeptic) must independently confirm or refute every finding, with verdicts backed by command output rather than reasoning alone.'
Protocol-doc discipline: the artifact contract, finding/verdict schemas, severity and signal-gate definitions, and provider adapter registry are normatively specified in docs/review-protocol.md.

competitors.name: linfangyu42/agentic-audit
key_points: Three orthogonal verification agents, one per dimension: verifier-depth (what's missing?), verifier-bias (what's wrong with the reasoning?), verifier-fact (what's factually incorrect?).

States the core empirical justification plainly: 'Single-agent self-audit is structurally unreliable. LLMs fail to detect their own errors ~64.5% of the time despite being able to correct the same errors in user-provided input.' — same figure as Self-Correction Bench (arXiv 2507.02778).
Design rules worth citing: 'External monitoring over self-monitoring — self-reflection is a trigger, not a corrector'; 'deliver the product, not the process'.
Requires the verifier agents to have web search access for fact-checking — an operational requirement most peers omit.

competitors.name: Arykozhang/adversarial-verify
key_points: The 'external verifier with zero prior memory' pattern taken to its logical end: package the whole project into a flat 20-file / 7-category brief (history, iterations, FAILED attempts, source, outputs, methodology, dataset) and hand it to an independent adversarial AI with a 4-axis mission document.

Key insight stated explicitly: 'The adversarial AI must have no prior memory of your project' — so you must package everything, including what was already tried and abandoned, to stop it re-suggesting dead ends.
Output grading P0 (blocking) / P1 (important) / P2 (optimization) with file references and fix specs plus acceptance criteria.

Field result worth citing as an anecdote: after fixes and cleanup, detection recall went 78% -> 87%; two P0 findings included a regex that missed nested generics (~6% missed detections) and a prompt that asked the LLM to check nulls without ever supplying type information.
Step 7 'interference cleanup' (purge stale agent scripts, expired system prompts, __pycache__, obsolete CSVs) is a genuinely unique step in the genre.

competitors.name: dsplce.co — Adversarial verification recipe (editorial competitor)
key_points: Best editorial treatment of the mechanism: the second opinion 'isn't one' if the same session provides it, because the model cross-checks against its own premises instead of re-deriving from the code.

Ran a control experiment: a senior-engineer-framed, deliberately FALSE finding about an empty-token auth bypass was correctly REJECTED by a fresh session — with four paragraphs, a code block, two caveats and an open question back to the human. Verdict: correct but unworkable at 40 findings, because 'it isn't a verification step at all, it's just 40 more things to read'.

Then shows the same finding through a purpose-built refuter: a single JSON verdict `{"refuted": true, "evidence": "<code>", "locator": "auth.py:1-10"}` — 'not extra cynicism, but a contract: a fixed decision rule and a fixed output shape'.

Five rules for a working refuter: pass the claim and not the conversation; do not include the first LLM's reasoning or a summary of it; do not disclose where the finding came from (authority framing is bias); DEFAULT TO REFUTATION (uncertainty is not a pass); fixed output schema.
Version-stamped (CLAUDE CODE 2.1.193 / CODEX CLI 0.146.0 / COPILOT CLI 1.0.77 / ANTIGRAVITY 1.1.9, verified 2026-08-03).

competitors.name: software-moling.com — 'Why AI Findings Need a Skeptic' (editorial competitor)
key_points: Best architectural write-up: analysis -> isolated fan-out verification -> voting threshold.
Isolation is the whole point: verifiers see only the finding and its cited evidence, never the analysis agent's reasoning chain — otherwise they inherit its biases.

Perspective-DIVERSE verification beats N identical refuters: 'Running multiple copies of the same verifier prompt reduces variance but not bias.' Roles suggested: correctness auditor, security reviewer (trust boundaries only), reproducibility auditor (can the finding be re-derived from cited evidence alone?).
Re-derivation is the gold standard for numeric claims: extract and execute the logic in a sandbox, compare numerically; 'the model cannot override a failed numeric check'.
Voting layer parameters: minimum verifier count and minimum survival rate; 2-of-3 is a reasonable floor for code review, unanimous for security/compliance where a single refutation should block.

Operational notes: context isolation is mandatory; token cost scales linearly (3 verifiers per finding triples the verification pass) — mitigate by parallelizing and by only routing high-confidence findings to full adversarial review.

Names three real failure modes: race condition mis-attributed to the wrong location; a numeric claim restated from the source rather than re-derived; an endpoint marked authenticated because an auth import was seen while the protection was registered in the wrong order.

stats.fact: 90% of professional developers now use AI at work, up 14% year over year, spending a median of two hours per day with AI tools; 71% use AI for writing new code.
stats.source: Google Cloud DORA, 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development (nearly 5,000 technology professionals) — https://cloud.google.com/resources/content/2025-dora-ai-assisted-software-development-report

stats.fact: The DORA 'trust paradox': only 24% of developers trust AI-generated output 'a lot' or 'a great deal', while 30% trust it 'a little' or 'not at all'; 49% trust it 'somewhat'. More than 80% still report productivity gains and 59% report improved code quality.
stats.source: Google Cloud DORA 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development

stats.fact: Autonomous agent adoption lags assisted AI sharply: only 17% of developers use agent mode daily and 61% never use autonomous agent mode, even though 80% report productivity improvements from assisted AI.
stats.source: Google Cloud DORA 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development (via DORA analysis summaries)

stats.fact: In organizations with weaker delivery practices, AI amplified dysfunction: delivery stability fell 7.2% and throughput declined 1.5% despite individual productivity gains.
stats.source: Google Cloud DORA 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development

stats.fact: 46% of developers actively distrust the accuracy of AI tools versus 33% who trust it, and only 3% report 'highly trusting' the output; distrust rose from 31% in 2024 while 84% use or plan to use AI tools.
stats.source: Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey — https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai

stats.fact: In a randomized controlled trial, 16 experienced open-source developers completed 246 real tasks 19% SLOWER when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools (Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet), while estimating afterwards that AI had made them 20% faster — a ~39-point gap between belief and measurement. Forecasts were +24% faster.
stats.source: METR, 'Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity', arXiv:2507.09089 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089

stats.fact: A February 2026 METR re-run with late-2025 tools still put returning developers at ~18% slower as the central estimate, with a confidence interval from -38% to +9%; METR characterizes the evidence for speedup as 'very weak' once selection effects are accounted for.
stats.source: METR follow-up study, February 2026 (via analysis summaries citing metr.org)

stats.fact: Across 623 million analyzed code changes (2023-2026), refactoring line moves fell 70%, long-term legacy maintenance fell 74% and cross-file function calls fell 35%, while within-commit copy/paste rose 41%, code block duplication rose 81% (40.3 -> 73.0 duplicated lines per million changed lines) and error-masking constructs rose 47%.
stats.source: GitClear, 'The Maintainability Gap: 2026 AI Code Quality Research' — https://www.gitclear.com/the_ai_code_quality_maintainability_gap

stats.fact: 2024 was the first year GitClear measured where within-commit 'copy/pasted' lines exceeded 'moved' (refactored) lines; the frequency of duplicated code blocks rose roughly eightfold, and refactoring activity dropped from 21% of changed lines in 2022 to under 10% in 2024.
stats.source: GitClear, 'AI Copilot Code Quality: 2025' (211 million changed lines, 2020-2024) — https://www.gitclear.com/ai_assistant_code_quality_2025_research

stats.fact: Prove It's own 12-case benchmark (codex-cli 0.147.0, gpt-5.6-luna, low reasoning, one run per cell, 2026-08-18) reports verdict accuracy rising from 75% baseline to 100% with the skill, positive-control accuracy 67% -> 100%, decisive-signal recall flat at 96%, and 0% false-assurance rate in both arms.
stats.source: Prove It repository, benchmark/README.md and benchmark/results/codex-gpt-5.6-luna-low-2026-08-18.json — authors state the cases were authored during skill development, so it is not an independent evaluation

stats.fact: Prove It repository scale at research time: 9 stars, 0 forks, 0 open issues, Apache-2.0, created and last pushed 2026-08-18, one release; listed on skills.sh. The nearest neighbor prove_it has 198 stars and bug-hunt 146 stars, so this is an early-stage skill in an already crowded niche.
stats.source: GitHub API repository metadata, retrieved 2026-10-01

stats.fact: 64.5% average 'Self-Correction Blind Spot' across 14 open-source non-reasoning models: LLMs reliably correct an error presented as external input but fail to correct the byte-identical error inside their own output.
stats.source: Self-Correction Bench, arXiv 2507.02778 (COLM 2026) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02778

stats.fact: Simply appending the word 'Wait' reduces the self-correction blind spot by 89.3% — evidence the capability exists but requires external activation, not new capability.
stats.source: Self-Correction Bench, arXiv 2507.02778 — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.02778

stats.fact: Models catch only 4.3%-10.8% of their own naturally generated errors when those errors are re-presented externally — the blind spot is not an artifact of injected test errors.
stats.source: Self-Correction Bench, arXiv 2507.02778 (Table 9) — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.02778

stats.fact: Relabeling a wrong claim from the agent's own reasoning into an external user message lifts the correction rate by 23 to 93 percentage points across 7 model families; a 'self-distrust' prompt that leaves the claim in place yields only 0-23% correction versus ~70% for the relabel. The failure is largely a harness/role-labeling artifact, which makes external re-presentation a controllable reliability lever.
stats.source: The Self-Correction Illusion: LLMs Correct Others but Not Themselves, arXiv 2606.05976 — https://arxiv.org/html/2606.05976v1

stats.fact: Intrinsic self-correction (no external feedback) often fails to improve and can DEGRADE reasoning accuracy — the canonical negative result behind 'let an external verifier decide'.
stats.source: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, Huang et al., arXiv 2310.01798 (ICLR 2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798

stats.fact: Tool-interactive critiquing (CRITIC) — where the critic calls external tools rather than re-reading its own prose — substantially improves factuality and code correctness; reliable external feedback is the condition under which self-correction works.
stats.source: CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing, arXiv 2305.11738 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738

stats.fact: Purpose-trained critic models find bugs in real-world code that human reviewers miss, and model critiques are preferred over human-written critiques in evaluation — the empirical basis for LLM-as-verifier.
stats.source: LLM Critics Help Catch LLM Bugs, McAleese et al. (OpenAI), arXiv 2407.00215 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00215

stats.fact: Multi-agent debate (multiple independent instances proposing and critiquing) improves factuality and reasoning over single-agent generation.
stats.source: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate, Du et al., arXiv 2305.14325 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325

stats.fact: Adversarial verification is a prover-verifier game: training a weaker verifier against a stronger prover yields outputs that are both correct and easier to check (legibility), rather than optimizing only for answer correctness.
stats.source: Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs, OpenAI, arXiv 2407.13692 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13692

stats.fact: Prove It's own reproducible 12-case benchmark, one directional run (Codex CLI 0.147.0, gpt-5.6-luna, low reasoning, 2026-08-18): correct verdict 9/12 (75%) baseline -> 12/12 (100%) with the skill; positive controls 2/3 (67%) -> 3/3 (100%); false-assurance rate 0/12 in both arms; falsification attempt rate 12/12 in both arms. Authors state it is a transparent regression test, not an independent evaluation.
stats.source: https://github.com/Pablo-aps/prove-it/blob/main/benchmark/README.md

angles: 'Vibe verification' is the named anti-pattern: an agent accumulates enough positive signals to feel confident and stops looking for ways its conclusion could be false. The skill's whole job is to reverse that search direction — falsify before you trust.

Signal vs outcome is the core distinction worth teaching: tests green != original bug fixed, build green != deployment works, deploy succeeded != every replica runs the new version, healthcheck 200 != system healthy, HTTP 200 != async operation completed, no ERROR lines != no relevant failure occurred.

Four verdicts as a calibrated scale: PROVEN is deliberately scoped (never formal correctness or future safety), FAILED requires direct contradiction, NOT PROVEN covers indirect/stale/narrow evidence, and BLOCKED is reserved for a named check that cannot run. This ordering prevents both blind trust and infinite skepticism.

Positive controls are the credibility test for a verification tool: a skill that always answers NOT PROVEN is useless, so the benchmark includes three cases that must return PROVEN and the skill explicitly warns against inventing unbounded hypothetical gaps after scope is covered.

Freeze the claim and acceptance criteria BEFORE inspecting evidence — otherwise verification degrades into moving the goalposts until the evidence fits. Prove It also treats its own prior conclusions as claims, not evidence.

Counterfeit proof taxonomy is the practical checklist: test.skip/xit, removed or weakened assertions, ignored exit codes, empty catches, `|| true`, blanket suppressions, hardcoded results, unrelated mocks, and timeout increases without a reproduced timing cause. These are not automatically wrong — they are evidence against a claim when they hide or redefine the behaviour being verified.
Read-only by default: verification must not mutate production, destroy data, weaken controls, or broaden authorization to obtain proof. The safest decisive check first, not the most dramatic.

Design tradeoff table: hook-enforced verification (prove_it), multi-agent adversarial panels (bug-hunt, cc-settings/verify), protocol-heavy CoV frameworks (claude-adversarial-skill), re-execution judges (fable-judge) and long-run orchestration (backpressured) versus a single portable SKILL.md with four rules and one verdict.

Why now: 90% AI adoption against 24% trust, 46% active distrust, and a measured 19% slowdown with a ~39-point perception gap — the failure mode is agents that are confident and wrong, exactly what an adversarial verification gate targets.

The maintainability context: with refactoring down 70% and duplication up 81% across 623M changes, 'it passed' matters less than 'it still holds' — verification has to check outcomes, not green signals.
Multi-model verification: all-Claude adversarial panels share blind spots, so a cross-model (Codex) finder is worth adding when the target is high blast radius (auth, crypto, payments, migrations).

Definition-first: most readers arrive not knowing 'adversarial verification' is a named architecture. Open by distinguishing it from (a) self-review, (b) ordinary code review, and (c) unit testing — the adversary's job is to REFUTE a specific claim, not to find more issues.

'Vibe verification' is the strongest ownable term in the topic: the moment an agent collects enough green signals to feel confident and stops looking for ways the conclusion could be false. Define it, show the swap ('Tests pass. Looks good.' vs 'What would let these tests pass while the bug still exists?').

Falsification-first framing, borrowed verbatim from prove-it's doctrine: don't try to prove it works, try to prove it doesn't. Frame the skill as changing the verification OBJECTIVE rather than the test framework — that's why it works across stacks.

Ground the mechanism in the 64.5% self-correction blind spot (arXiv 2507.02778) and the 23-93pp relabel lift (arXiv 2606.05976): a same-session 'double-check' is not a second opinion, it is a consistency check against its own premises. This is the article's intellectual spine and the reason a fresh-context verifier is mandatory rather than stylistic.

The verdict vocabulary is the real product: PROVEN / FAILED / NOT PROVEN / BLOCKED. Spend a section on why NOT PROVEN is the most valuable of the four — it is the honest answer for indirect, incomplete, stale or narrow evidence, and it is the verdict that collapses into a false 'done' in every naive agent loop.

Counterfeit proof taxonomy as the practical centerpiece: skipped tests, weakened assertions, ignored exit codes, empty catches, hardcoded results, behavior mocked away, timeouts increased without reproducing the timing failure. Give the reader a copy-pasteable pre-flight checklist.

'A passing signal is not a passing outcome' — the proxies-vs-outcomes table (exit code != fix, build green != deployment, deploy ok != every replica, healthcheck 200 != workers healthy, HTTP 200 != async job completed, one request != race fixed). Highly quotable and directly reusable as a table.

Show the install/invoke reality across three agents (Claude Code `/prove-it`, Codex `$prove-it`, Cursor) via `npx skills add Pablo-aps/prove-it` — a true how-to needs the 30-second install and one real invocation example, plus the auto-activation trigger words (prove, verify, validate, confirm, double-check).

Be honest about the evidence: the 75% -> 100% benchmark is one directional run on a self-authored 12-case suite. Present it as a reproducible regression test, cite the SHA-256-fingerprinted methodology, and pair it with independent academic evidence instead of overselling the vendor number. This honesty is itself an angle — it models the skill's own doctrine.

Cost and threshold engineering, which almost every competitor article skips: adversarial verification is not free (3 verifiers per finding triples the verification pass). Cover triage (route only high-confidence findings to full adversarial review), 2-of-3 as the code-review floor, unanimous for security/compliance, and tightening thresholds when escaped defects surface.

Comparison section is mandatory for this keyword cluster: prove-it (adjudicates a claim) vs bug-hunt (Hunter/Skeptic/Referee hunt) vs production-audit (24-lens convergence) vs Sub-Zero (fresh-context world check) vs fullo/claude-adversarial-skill (CoV + tri-modal confidence) vs ng/adversarial-review (cross-vendor Optimizer/Skeptic). Position, don't rank.

Name-collision story as a hook: at least six unrelated repos named 'prove-it' shipped between 2026-04 and 2026-09 (Pablo-aps, jkaraml, josharsh, jongouveia, ryanda9910, dvhthomas). The name converged before the design did — evidence the need is real and the pattern is not yet standardized.

The trust-gap framing for the intro/outro: 84% adoption against 29% trust; 93% of orgs had a root cause misdiagnosed by an AI hallucination in six months. The skill is a cheap, local control on an expensive failure mode — a process fix, not a prompt trick.

Add the anti-pattern warning competitors omit: adversarially verify the VERIFIER too. Isolation, default-refuted, read-only, and frozen acceptance criteria are the safety rails; a verifier that can mutate production to obtain proof, or that relaxes the claim after a failed check, is worse than no verifier because it manufactures false assurance.
